newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Cocoa still flimsy, coffee to hold.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Cocoa still flimsy, coffee to hold.

text.p: Cocoa futures may eye key support at 1,000 stg a tonne basis September after last week's failure to make much impression on the upside in reaction to the recent large fund sell-off, traders said.
The main impetus for the market should come from speculative funds, the net long holders in the market, and also movements in sterling.
In other softs markets, robusta coffee was expected to consolidate at just above $1,600 basis September after last week's sharp fall on heavy fund long liquidation.
In white sugar, traders bemoaned the lack of fundamental news and said market direction hinged on the action of investment funds in the New York raws market.
London's cocoa market drew some support on Friday on second-quarter U.S. cocoa grind data, which came in higher than expected.
But the rise was short-lived. The benchmark September contract finished Friday nine stg down at 1,015 per tonne, the week's low.

"It was just a 10-minute wonder," said one physical trader. "But it's an encouraging sign -- I am quite pleased and with the kind of cold, damp summer in Europe, it should help European (chocolate) consumption as well."
The U.S. grind rose by 17.54 percent to 97,223 tonnes in the second quarter 1997 from the same period in 1996.
One negative factor for LIFFE cocoa was the persistent strength of sterling against the U.S. dollar and major European units.
"The strong sterling makes this market even more difficult," another trader said.
The futures market was also vulnerable to another downward retracement on speculative long liquidation, market sources said.
Robusta coffee futures should try to consolidate at just above $1,600 after last week's sharp falls.
Support was seen at $1,530, the low on July 16 when the market came under severe fund-led long liquidation. An immediate upside hurdle was pegged at $1,650.
Last week's fund shake-out came despite what many traders described as the absence of strong Far East origin selling and a calm New York arabicas market.
But the fund selling had dwindled, at least for now, and traders said speculators and funds were probably looking to buy November after the July expiry.

Dealers in London's white sugar futures market said the recent disruption by South African sugar workers, flood damage to crops in Poland and the Thai drought, which was expected to cause a sharp fall in output, had so far failed to have any real effect on the market, they said.
The outlook for the London market depended heavily on what the funds did in New York, traders said.
"Funds seem happy to stay with big long positions," one trader said.
"Any sign of strength and they rush back. It will take a monumental drop in the market to flush them out." -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
